blocks.title: Basic facts
head: Point
Fact

First, a Paris workshop on national human rights bodies (October 1991). Then the Human Rights Ordinance (28 September 1993). Then the NHRC was set up (12 October 1993). Finally the Act got the President's assent (8 January 1994).

To support and strengthen efforts already being made. (Replacing courts or punishing violators was NOT an objective.)

blocks.title: Key extra points
items: NCW was recommended by the Committee on the Status of Women in India (1974) and the National Perspective Plan for Women (1988).
NCW has a 14-point mandate (list of duties). It includes inspecting jails and remand homes where women are kept, and funding court cases that affect many women.
NCW can look into complaints and can also take notice of a violation of women's rights on its own (suo motu), without waiting for a complaint.
NCW's innovation: Parivarik Mahila Lok Adalat (family women's people's court) for quick, free settlement of marriage and family disputes.
'Minority' is not defined in the Constitution, and the NCM Act does not define it either. The Central government notifies minorities for the Act.
Notified minorities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Zoroastrians (Parsis) in 1993; Jains were added in 2014, so there are now 6. Parsis are the smallest minority.
NCM is statutory, not constitutional. The Constitution itself protects religious and linguistic minorities (Articles 29 and 30).
Under the child rights law, a child is a person below 18 years. This follows the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (20 November 1989), which India ratified on 11 December 1992.

NCPCR also has duties under the Right to Education (RTE) Act 2009, the POCSO Act 2012 (protection of children from sexual offences) and the Juvenile Justice Act 2015. It cannot take up a matter already pending before a State commission for child rights.
Children's Courts: a Court of Session chosen by the State with the agreement of the High Court Chief Justice; a special public prosecutor must have 7 years' practice.

sections.heading: Origin: right to know and the history of RTI

blocks.title: What kind of right is it?
items: Fundamental right: the Supreme Court has read the right to information into Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression). You cannot speak or vote wisely without knowing facts.
Laxmikanth lists 'right to know about government activities' under Article 19(1)(a) and 'right to information' among the rights read into Article 21 (right to life).
Legal right: the RTI Act, 2005 gives the actual procedure. So RTI in India is BOTH a fundamental right and a legal (statutory) right.
Main aim of the Act: transparency (openness) and accountability (answerability) in every public authority, and so to reduce corruption.
Under Section 3, the right is given to all CITIZENS – not to foreigners, and not to companies as bodies in their own name.

items.what: Sweden – first country in the world to give a legal right to information
Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), Article 19 – the UN treats freedom to seek and receive information as a human right
State of U.P. v. Raj Narain – Supreme Court: people have a right to know every public act done by public officials; this flows from Article 19(1)(a)
Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS) formed in Rajasthan by Aruna Roy; its public hearings (jan sunwai) on village accounts started the RTI movement
Tamil Nadu (first state) and Goa pass state RTI laws, before any national law

RTI Act, 2005 enacted (date of President's assent). Some sections started at once
items.detail: It repealed (cancelled) the Freedom of Information Act, 2002

items.what: Rest of the RTI Act came into force – on the 120th day after enactment. Central Information Commission set up in 2005

RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019: the Central Government now fixes the term and salary of Information Commissioners. Also in 2019, the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 repealed (cancelled) the J&K RTI Act, 2009, so the central RTI Act now applies to Jammu and Kashmir
Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023: Section 44(3) of this Act rewrote Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act (the exemption for personal information)

blocks.text: Order of the four laws: Freedom of Information Act (2002), then RTI Act (2005), then Whistle Blowers Protection Act (2014), then DPDP Act (2023).

sections.heading: Key sections of the RTI Act, 2005

blocks.title: Section-wise
head: Section
What it says
rows: 'Public authority' = a body set up by the Constitution, by a law of Parliament or a State Legislature, or by a government notification or order. It also covers a non-government body (even an NGO) that is owned, controlled or substantially financed by the government. A private firm with no government money or control is NOT a public authority.
Information about a PRIVATE body can be obtained only through a public authority that can get that information under some law in force.

'Right to information' includes: inspecting works, documents and records; taking notes and certified copies; taking certified samples of material; getting information in electronic form (floppies, tapes, etc.).
'Third party' = any person other than the citizen asking for information; it can include a public authority.
All citizens have the right to information.

Duties of public authorities, including proactive disclosure (suo motu – publishing on its own, without any request). Under Section 4(1)(b) each authority must publish, without being asked, things like the powers and duties of its officers, its budget, and its PIO's contact details – so that people need to file fewer RTI applications.
Every public authority appoints Public Information Officers (PIOs – the officers who supply information) and Assistant PIOs (who receive applications and forward them).

How to apply: in writing or electronically, in English, Hindi or the official language of the area. The applicant need NOT give any reason, nor any personal details except those needed to contact him.
Time limits for reply (see next section). If no reply comes in time, the request is treated as rejected ('deemed refusal'), and the applicant can appeal.
Exemptions – information that need not be given (see Exemptions section).
Third-party information – the third party is given notice and heard before disclosure.
Central Information Commission: how it is set up, term of office of members, and their removal
State Information Commission: how it is set up, term of office of members, and their removal
Appeals – first appeal and second appeal
The RTI Act overrides (prevails over) the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and other laws, to the extent they are inconsistent.
Act does not apply to listed intelligence and security organisations (see Exemptions section).

blocks.title: Who runs the Act
items: In each central office, the Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) is the officer who actually handles RTI requests.
Nodal agency at the Centre: Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), Ministry of Personnel.
The Act applies to BOTH the Central and State Governments; it created both the Central and State Information Commissions, and it provides penalties.

blocks.title: Must receive and inquire into a complaint (Section 18) from any person who
items: could not submit a request because no PIO was appointed;
was refused the information;
got no reply within the time limit;
thinks the fee charged is unreasonable;
thinks the information given is incomplete, misleading or false;
has any other problem in obtaining information.
Not covered: claims like compensation for a service defect by a private company – that is not an information matter.

blocks.title: Other powers
items: Suo motu (on its own) power: it can order an inquiry into any matter if there are reasonable grounds.

While inquiring, it has the powers of a CIVIL COURT under the Code of Civil Procedure: summoning persons and making them give evidence on oath and produce documents; discovery and inspection of documents; receiving evidence on affidavit; requisitioning (calling for) public records from any court or office; issuing summons for witnesses or documents.
It can examine any record held by the public authority, and NO record can be withheld from it on any ground – not even national security.
It has NO power to imprison anyone.

blocks.title: To secure compliance it can require the public authority to
items: give access to information in a particular form;
appoint a PIO where none exists;
publish information or categories of information;
change its practices of managing, keeping and destroying records;
give more RTI training to officials;
give an annual report on compliance;
compensate the applicant for any loss or harm suffered.
It can also impose penalties and reject an application. It CANNOT dismiss the head of a department.

blocks.title: Penalty (Section 20)
items: On the defaulting PIO (not the head of department): Rs 250 per day of delay, up to a maximum of Rs 25,000.
Example: 60 days' delay at Rs 250 per day = Rs 15,000.
It can also recommend disciplinary action against the PIO.
When a public authority does not follow the Act, the Commission may only RECOMMEND steps to it – this recommendation is not binding like a court decree.

blocks.text: Role: the Commission is the second appellate authority (the body that hears the second appeal), and only on matters of information. It does not itself solve the citizen's underlying grievance (for example, it will not release a pending pension).

States that already had a Lokayukta did not have to rewrite their laws to copy the Lokpal.

blocks.title: Basic facts
items: Full form: National Institution for Transforming India ('Aayog' means commission).
On 13 August 2014 the Government announced that the Planning Commission, which was then 65 years old, would be scrapped (closed down).
NITI Aayog was set up on 1 January 2015 as the successor of the Planning Commission.
It was created by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet (a government order) — not by the Constitution and not by an Act of Parliament.
So it is neither a constitutional body nor a statutory body. It only gives advice: it is the Government's main policy 'think tank' (a group of experts that studies problems and suggests policies).

It does not make Five-Year Plans. It follows a 'bottom-up' approach: planning starts from villages and States and moves up, and States are treated as equal partners. This is called cooperative federalism.
Cooperative federalism (Centre and States working together) got new importance after NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission, because Chief Ministers sit in its Governing Council.

sections.heading: Planning Commission (1950–2014) and how NITI differs

blocks.title: Planning Commission — key facts
items: Set up in March 1950 by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet.
It was set up on the recommendation of the Advisory Planning Board (1946) headed by K.C. Neogi.
It was neither constitutional nor statutory, so critics called it an extra-constitutional body.
It was the top body for planning in India. But legally it was only a staff agency (an advisory body) and had no executive power (no power to make decisions binding on the Government).
Chairman: Prime Minister. The Deputy Chairman was its de facto (actual working) head.
Pranab Mukherjee was Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission (1991–1996) and later became President of India (2012–2017).
The Secretary of the Planning Commission also worked as the Secretary of the NDC.
States had no representation in it — it was wholly a Centre-made body.
Critics called it a 'Super Cabinet', 'Economic Cabinet', 'Parallel Cabinet' and 'Fifth Wheel of the Coach'.

blocks.title: Why it was said to weaken fiscal federalism
items: The Finance Commission (Art 280) is called the 'balancing wheel of fiscal federalism' (fiscal federalism means sharing of money between the Centre and States). Till 2014 its role was weakened by the Planning Commission, because the Planning Commission also gave large grants to States.
P.V. Rajamannar (Chairman of the Fourth Finance Commission) said the functions of the Planning Commission and Finance Commission overlapped.
K. Santhanam said planning had 'superseded the federation', making India work like a unitary (centralised) system.

Note for Assertion–Reason questions: it is true that the Planning Commission was made by an executive resolution, and that is why it was called extra-constitutional. But the charge that it weakened federalism came mainly from its grant-giving role. So both statements are true, but the Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

head: Clause

For 15 years from the start of the Constitution (1950 to 1965), English continues for all Union official purposes for which it was used before 1950.
Even after 15 years, Parliament may by law allow English for specified purposes. This is an ordinary law: Art 343 itself gives this power, so the Art 368 amendment procedure is not needed.

items: Purpose: to review how far Hindi is being used for Union official work, and to report to the President.
Members: 30 MPs, 20 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha, elected by each House by proportional representation with single transferable vote.
The Act allowed it to be formed only after 10 years from 26 January 1965; it was actually set up in 1976.
The President lays its report before each House of Parliament and sends it to all State Governments. After that, the President may issue directions based on the report.
Its Chairman is elected by its members. By convention (established practice, not a written rule), the Union Home Minister is elected Chairman.
Its office staff (secretariat) works as a subordinate office of the Department of Official Language in the Ministry of Home Affairs.

sections.heading: Regional languages and language of the legislatures (Art 345–347, Art 120, Art 210)

blocks.text: The Constitution does not name the official language of any State. Each State chooses its own.

head: Article
Rule
rows: A State legislature may adopt one or more languages used in the State, or Hindi, as its official language. Until it does so, English continues. The choice need not be from the Eighth Schedule.

The Union's official language (in practice, English) is the language used for communication between the Union and a State, and between one State and another. Two or more States may agree to use Hindi for communication between themselves.

First, a demand must be made. If the President is then satisfied that a substantial part of a State's people want the language they speak to be recognised, he may direct that this language also be officially recognised in that State. This protects linguistic minorities.

Business in Parliament is done in Hindi or in English. The presiding officer (Speaker of Lok Sabha or Chairman of Rajya Sabha) may let a member who cannot express himself or herself in Hindi or English speak in the mother tongue. The words 'or in English' were to drop out after 15 years, unless Parliament by law decided otherwise. Continuing English therefore needs only an ordinary law of Parliament (the 1963 Act did this), not a constitutional amendment under Art 368.

Business in a State legislature is done in the State's official language(s), Hindi or English. The presiding officer (Speaker or Chairman) may let a member speak in the mother tongue. The State legislature decides whether English continues after 15 years (25 years for Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura; 40 years for Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram).

blocks.title: Official Languages Act 1963 on communication
items: English is used between the Union and non-Hindi States (States that have not adopted Hindi).
When Hindi is used between a Hindi State and a non-Hindi State, an English translation must go with it.

sections.heading: Language of the courts and of laws (Art 348–349, Art 394A)

blocks.title: Art 348
head: Item
Rule
rows: Supreme Court and High Court proceedings
In English only, until Parliament provides otherwise. Parliament has made no law for Hindi in the Supreme Court.
Authoritative (legally binding) texts of Bills, Acts, Ordinances, orders, rules, regulations and bye-laws
In English, for both Central and State laws

The Governor, with the President's previous (advance) consent, may allow Hindi or the State's official language in High Court proceedings. This does NOT cover the High Court's judgements, decrees and orders.
The State legislature may use a language other than English for its Bills and Acts, but an English translation must also be published, and that translation is the authoritative text

blocks.title: Official Languages Act 1963 and later laws
items: The Act lets the Governor, with the President's previous (advance) consent, allow Hindi or the State's official language for High Court judgements, decrees and orders. An English translation must be attached to each.

A Hindi translation of a Central Act, published under the President's authority, is treated as its authoritative (legally accepted) Hindi text. Every Bill introduced in Parliament must also carry a Hindi translation.

Authorised Translations (Central Laws) Act 1973: when the President publishes in the official Gazette a translation of a Central law into an Eighth Schedule language other than Hindi, that translation is the authoritative text in that language.

blocks.title: Art 349 and Art 394A
items: Art 349: during the first 15 years (1950 to 1965), no Bill or amendment changing the language of courts and laws (the matters in Art 348(1)) could be introduced in Parliament without the President's previous sanction (advance permission). The President could give this sanction only after considering the Official Language Commission's recommendations and the Committee of Parliament's report.
Art 394A (in Part XXII), inserted by the 58th Amendment Act, 1987: the PRESIDENT (not the Governor) has the authoritative Hindi translation of the Constitution, and of every amendment, published.

sections.heading: Special directives: linguistic minorities and Hindi (Art 350, 350A, 350B, 351)

head: Article
Provision
Origin
rows: Every person may send a written complaint (representation) to any Union or State officer or authority to get a grievance solved, in any language used in the Union or the State. This right belongs to every aggrieved person, not only to linguistic minorities.

Every State, and every local authority in the State, shall try (endeavour) to give adequate facilities for teaching in the mother tongue at the primary school stage to children of linguistic minority groups. The President may issue directions to any State to secure these facilities.
7th Amendment, 1956 (on the recommendation of the States Reorganisation Commission)

The President appoints a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities. The Officer investigates all matters about the safeguards for linguistic minorities and reports to the President. The President lays these reports before each House of Parliament and sends them to the State governments concerned.

The Union has a duty to spread and develop Hindi, so that it can express all elements of India's composite (mixed, shared) culture. Hindi is to be enriched by taking in forms and style from Hindustani and the Eighth Schedule languages, and taking its vocabulary mainly from Sanskrit.

blocks.title: Background: bodies on language and States (before the 7th Amendment)
items: Dhar Commission (Linguistic Provinces Commission), June 1948, chaired by S.K. Dhar: preferred administrative convenience over language as the basis for forming States.
JVP Committee, December 1948 (Congress): Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya; it also rejected language as the basis (report April 1949).
States Reorganisation Commission, December 1953, chaired by Fazl Ali (members K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru): broadly accepted language as the basis; its report led to the 7th Amendment, 1956.
Official Language Commission, 1955: chaired by B.G. Kher (different from the bodies above, which dealt with forming States).

blocks.title: Special Officer = Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (CLM)
items: It is a constitutional body, because Art 350B creates it. The office was created in 1957.
The Constitution does not fix the Officer's qualifications, term of office, salary or method of removal.
Headquarters: New Delhi. Regional offices: Belgaum, Chennai and Kolkata.
Works under the Union Ministry of Minority Affairs, and sends its reports to the President through the Union Minister of Minority Affairs.

Compare: NITI Aayog (set up by an executive resolution of the government), the National Commission for Minorities (statutory, under a 1992 Act) and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC, statutory, under a 1993 Act) are NOT constitutional bodies.

blocks.title: Who is a linguistic minority?
items: A group whose mother tongue differs from that of the majority in the State or part of the State.
Linguistic minorities are decided State by State. So Telugu speakers are a linguistic minority in Karnataka, even though Telugu is a major Indian language.

blocks.title: Linguistic safeguards in other Parts
head: Article
Safeguard
rows: Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve (protect and keep) it
Minorities, whether religious or linguistic, may establish and run educational institutions of their choice
Claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to government services and posts. This is not a language article: it is in Part XVI, while Art 350A and Art 351 are in Part XVII.

National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Art 338), for Scheduled Tribes (Art 338A) and for Backward Classes (Art 338B). Compare with Art 350B, which creates the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages (14 originally): Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santhali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu. Bhojpuri is NOT in it (as of Nov 2026).

blocks.title: Why the Schedule matters and how it changes
items: Members of the Official Language Commission are chosen to represent these languages (Art 344).
Their forms, style and expressions are used to enrich Hindi (Art 351).

Adding a language needs a constitutional amendment under Art 368, passed by a special majority of Parliament. Ratification (approval) by half the State legislatures is NOT required, because the Eighth Schedule is not in the list of matters in the proviso to Art 368(2).
No language added since the 92nd Amendment, 2003 (as of Nov 2026).

blocks.title: Criteria (as in Laxmikanth)
items: High antiquity (great age): its early texts or recorded history go back 1500 to 2000 years.
A body of ancient literature valued as heritage by generations of speakers.
An original literary tradition of its own, not borrowed from another language community.
The classical language and literature are different from the modern form; there may even be a break (discontinuity) between the classical form and its later forms.

items: Official language: Telugu, under the Andhra Pradesh Official Languages Act, 1966 (made under Art 345).
Urdu was earlier the second official language in 15 districts of undivided Andhra Pradesh.

Art 343(1): the Union's language is Hindi in Devanagari script, but the numerals are the international form (1, 2, 3), not Devanagari numerals.
Kher Commission was set up in 1955 and reported in 1956; the Pant Committee examined it in 1957. The second Commission due in 1960 was never appointed.

Under Art 348, the Governor can allow Hindi in High Court proceedings but NOT in its judgements. Hindi judgements are possible only under the 1963 Act, with an English translation. The Supreme Court works in English only.
Art 350 was in the original Constitution and applies to every person. Art 350A and Art 350B were added by the 7th Amendment, 1956.
